title: From Pollination to Fertilisation in Flowering Plants
summary: A recap of pollination, the growth of the pollen tube, double fertilisation, and the changes in the flower afterwards.

p: Recall that the flower is the sexual reproductive organ of a flowering plant. The stamen (anther and filament) is the male part. The carpel (stigma, style and ovary with ovules) is the female part. Pollination is the transfer of mature pollen grains from the anther to the stigma. Self-pollination (for example tomato) is within the same flower or plant; cross-pollination (for example pawpaw) is between flowers of different plants of the same species and gives healthier and more varied offspring.

Insect-pollinated flowers (hibiscus, pride of Barbados) are large, coloured and scented, have nectar, a sticky stigma and rough sticky pollen. Wind-pollinated flowers (maize, grasses, rice) are small, dull and scentless, have anthers and feathery stigmas hanging outside, and make light, smooth pollen in huge amounts. Wind pollen is plentiful because most of it is lost and only a few grains land on a stigma by chance.
Pollination only brings the pollen to the stigma. Fertilisation is the fusion of the gametes.

1. Germination of pollen: a pollen grain landing on a compatible stigma takes in a sugary liquid and swells. 2. Pollen tube growth: the grain grows a tube that pushes down through the style towards the ovary, with the male nuclei inside. 3. Entry: the tube enters the ovule through a tiny pore called the micropyle. 4. Double fertilisation: one male nucleus fuses with the egg cell to form the zygote (the future plant), and the other fuses with the two polar nuclei (the secondary nucleus) to form a triploid (3n) nucleus, which becomes the endosperm (food store). Two fusions occur, so it is called double fertilisation; it is a special feature of flowering plants.

img.alt: A longitudinal section of a carpel showing pollen grains on the stigma, a pollen tube growing down the style into the ovule through the micropyle, with the egg cell, polar nuclei and embryo sac labelled
img.cap: The growth of the pollen tube and fertilisation. (The diagram spells 'polar nuclei' as 'pollar nuclei'; the correct spelling is polar.)

p: The petals and sepals usually wither and fall off. The stigma and style also wither. The changes are summarised below.

Why do the petals fall off while tomato seeds form inside the fruit? Because the petals have finished their job of attracting pollinators. The plant then sends its food and energy to the ovary to grow the fruit and seeds, instead of wasting it on the petals.

title: The Structure of Seeds: Bean and Maize
summary: Monocot and dicot seeds, the parts of a bean seed, and the maize grain as a fruit with its scutellum and coleoptile.

sections.h: A seed is a ripened ovule
p: A seed is a ripened, fertilised ovule that contains the embryo plant with a store of food. Monocotyledonous seeds (maize, rice, wheat) have one cotyledon (seed leaf), and the food is mostly stored in a separate endosperm. Dicotyledonous seeds (bean, groundnut, mango) have two cotyledons, which are large and store the food (starch and protein).

Testa: the tough brown seed coat, which protects against fungi, bacteria and insects. Hilum: a scar showing where the seed was joined to the pod. Micropyle: a tiny pore near the hilum, through which water and air enter when the seed germinates. Embryo: made of the plumule (the young shoot, with the epicotyl above the cotyledons), the radicle (the young root) and the hypocotyl (the stem part below the cotyledons). Cotyledons: two large fleshy 'seed leaves' that store food.

img.alt: A bean seed cut open showing the seed coat, two cotyledons, epicotyl, hypocotyl and radicle forming the embryo

p: A maize 'seed' is actually a whole fruit called a caryopsis (grain), because the fruit wall (pericarp) is joined tightly to the seed coat. Endosperm: the large yellow part that stores starch. Scutellum: the single cotyledon, which lies between the endosperm and the embryo and absorbs digested food from the endosperm for the growing embryo. Coleoptile: a sheath that protects the young shoot (plumule). Coleorhiza: a sheath that protects the young root (radicle).
How to see it: soak maize grains for a day, cut one lengthwise with a blade, and put a drop of iodine on the cut face. The endosperm turns blue-black, showing starch. Draw and label it.

title: Germination of Seeds
summary: The conditions needed for germination, epigeal and hypogeal germination, dormancy and a home experiment.

p: Germination is the waking of the embryo from its resting stage (dormancy) so that it grows into a seedling. Dry seeds have very little water and respire very slowly.

Water: to soften the testa, make the cells swell and start the enzymes working to digest the stored food. Oxygen: for respiration, which releases energy for growth (seeds in waterlogged soil may rot). Warmth: a suitable temperature, usually about 25 to 35 °C, for enzymes to work. Light is not normally needed for the first stages (a few seeds, such as some weeds, need light). Soil is also not needed, as seeds germinate on wet cotton wool.

The cotyledons are carried above the ground. The hypocotyl (the stem part below the cotyledons) grows rapidly and forms an arch that pulls the cotyledons out of the soil. Examples: bean, melon, castor oil, groundnut, cowpea, morning glory. After the first true leaves open, the cotyledons shrink as the food is used, turn green for a short time and then wither and fall off.
The cotyledons stay under the ground. The epicotyl (the stem part above the cotyledons) grows quickly and pushes the shoot up. Examples: maize, guinea corn (sorghum), millet, pea, yam seed.
Study the table.

sections.h: Dormancy and how farmers break it
p: Dormancy is a resting stage in which a living seed does not germinate even when conditions are right. It lets seeds survive the dry season. Farmers can break it by soaking in water, scratching or nicking the hard seed coat (scarification), soaking in warm water, dipping in weak acid, or exposing to cold. Test your seeds first: put 20 in wet cotton wool and count how many germinate (germination percentage).

Home project: plant 5 bean seeds and 5 maize seeds in two tins. Watch for 7 days. In bean you will see a loop (the hypocotyl arch) and fat cotyledons coming out first; in maize the green spear-like shoot comes out and the grain stays in the soil.

title: Fruits: Structure and Classification
summary: What a fruit is, the three layers of the pericarp, true and false fruits, simple, aggregate and multiple fruits, and the fleshy and dry types.

p: A fruit is a fertilised, ripened ovary that contains seeds. After fertilisation, the ovary swells and changes to protect the seeds and help to scatter them. In cooking, 'fruit' means something sweet, but in biology tomatoes, okra, pepper and cucumber are all fruits, because they develop from flowers and contain seeds.

The wall of a fruit is the pericarp. In many fleshy fruits it has three layers: the epicarp (the outer skin or peel), the mesocarp (the middle, usually fleshy and edible layer) and the endocarp (the inner layer around the seed, sometimes hard and stony).

True fruit: made from the ovary only. Examples: mango, orange, cowpea. False fruit (pseudocarp): made from the ovary together with other parts of the flower. Examples: apple (the flesh is the swollen receptacle), cashew (the 'apple' is the swollen stalk; the true fruit is the kidney-shaped nut hanging under it), strawberry (the red flesh is the receptacle; the real fruits are the tiny dots on it) and pineapple.

Simple fruit: from one flower with one ovary, for example bean, cherry, tomato. Aggregate fruit: from one flower with many separate ovaries, each becoming a small fruitlet in a cluster, for example strawberry and custard apple. Multiple (composite) fruit: from a whole cluster of flowers (an inflorescence) that fuse together, for example pineapple and breadfruit.

Berry: the whole pericarp is soft and juicy, usually with many seeds. Examples: tomato, pepper, guava, watermelon, and orange (a special berry called a hesperidium). Drupe: a fleshy mesocarp and a hard stony endocarp (a stone) around one seed. Examples: mango, coconut (a fibrous drupe), oil palm fruit, cherry. Pome: the outer flesh is the receptacle and the core is the real ovary. Examples: apple, pear.

img.alt: A diagram comparing a tomato (berry), a cherry (drupe) and an apple (pome) in section
img.cap: A berry, a drupe and a pome.

p: Dry dehiscent fruits split open when ripe to let out the seeds. Legume (pod): splits along two sides; bean, cowpea, flamboyant. Capsule: splits along many lines or pores; okra, cotton, poppy. Follicle: splits along one side only; kola, rose periwinkle. Schizocarp: breaks into one-seeded parts; Desmodium, Cassia.

Dry indehiscent fruits do not split. Caryopsis (grain): the seed coat is fused to the fruit wall; maize, rice, grasses. Cypsela: a small one-seeded fruit often with a hairy parachute (pappus); Tridax, sunflower. Nut: a very hard woody pericarp; cashew nut. Samara: a fruit wall with a wing; Combretum.

A maize grain is called a fruit, not just a seed, because the fruit wall is joined to the seed coat. A berry and a drupe differ in how the seed is protected: in a drupe a hard stony endocarp surrounds a single seed; in a berry the seeds lie in soft flesh with no stone.

title: Seed and Fruit Dispersal and Parthenocarpy
summary: Why seeds are dispersed, the four methods (wind, water, animals and explosive) with their adaptations, and fruits that form without fertilisation.

p: Dispersal is the scattering of seeds away from the parent plant. It prevents overcrowding, reduces competition for light, water and minerals, helps plants to colonise new places, and reduces the spread of disease among crowded seedlings.

img.alt: An infographic showing seed dispersal by wind, expulsion, animals and water with examples

p: Adaptations: very small and light seeds (orchids); wings, as in the samara of Combretum and Terminalia; parachutes of hairs (pappus) as in Tridax, dandelion and cotton seeds; plumes and flat shapes. Wind-dispersed fruits are dry and light.

Adaptations: buoyancy so that they float; a waterproof outer layer (epicarp) so that they do not rot; air spaces in a fibrous mesocarp that trap air. Examples: coconut (which can float across oceans and so grows on coasts), water lily, mangrove.

Edible fruits: bright colour, sweet smell and tasty pulp attract animals, which eat them and drop the seeds far away in their dung, where the seeds pass through the gut unharmed (guava, tomato, pepper, pawpaw, bats and birds spread many trees). Hooks and spines catch on fur or clothes (Desmodium, Boerhavia, the 'black-jack' Bidens pilosa, Triumfetta).

The fruit wall dries unevenly and builds up tension. When it is ripe and dry, it bursts open suddenly, 'shooting' the seeds away. Examples: oil bean (Pentaclethra), balsam, rubber seed, okra, and many pods. This throws seeds only a short distance, so they do not travel as far as wind-dispersed seeds.

sections.h: Why unripe fruits are green and sour
p: Unripe fruits are green, hard and sour, so that animals do not eat them before the seeds are ready. When the seeds are mature, the fruit changes colour, becomes sweet and smells nice, so animals are attracted and spread the seeds.

Parthenocarpy is the formation of a fruit without fertilisation, so the fruit has no seeds (it is seedless). Examples: banana and some pineapples. Farmers can cause it by spraying the flowers with plant hormones (auxins) to make seedless grapes, tomatoes or watermelons. This is useful for eating, but the plant cannot reproduce by seed, so banana is grown from suckers.

activity: Collect five weed seeds from around your house or school and say how each is dispersed. State three adaptations of wind-dispersed seeds. Explain why a coconut is adapted for water dispersal. Why do explosive fruits not spread as far as wind-dispersed ones?

title: Courtship Behaviour in Animals
summary: Why animals perform courtship, with examples of visual, sound, chemical and territorial displays, including the Agama lizard and the peacock.

p: Reproduction is not only about body parts. It also needs behaviour that makes sure the right mates meet and the young survive. These behaviours are mostly instinctive (inborn): the animal does not need to learn them.
Courtship is the series of special actions that a male and female of the same species perform to excite each other before mating.

1. Species recognition: it makes sure animals mate with their own kind; a female lizard will not respond to the dance of a male toad, so no effort is wasted on mating that would produce no young. 2. Synchronisation: it prepares both partners so that the female releases her eggs at the right time that the male releases sperm. 3. Mate selection: the female can choose a strong, healthy male with good genes (survival of the fittest). 4. Territory: it sets up a safe place for mating and nesting and shows that the male can defend it.

Visual: bright colours and movements. The male rainbow agama lizard (Agama agama), so common on Nigerian walls and trees, shows an orange-red head with a blue body (the female is a duller brown), nods its head rapidly (head-bobbing) and does 'push-ups'. The male peacock spreads its large, colourful tail feathers in front of the peahen.
Sound: frogs and toads croak loudly in the rainy season, and birds sing special mating songs. Crickets chirp.

Chemical (pheromones): a pheromone is a chemical signal released by an animal that affects the behaviour of another of the same species. Female moths release pheromones that males can smell kilometres away; dogs and cats mark territory and show readiness with urine.
Territorial: fighting and threatening to win and hold a breeding ground, for example male agamas, cocks and antelope.

The lesson note says the male agama has a 'bright blue head and orange tail'. In the common Nigerian rainbow agama it is the other way round: the head is orange-red and the body and tail base are blue. If your own lizards look different, remember that colours can vary between places and species, and always describe what you really see.
It keeps the species going, because animals must find a mate. It passes on good genes. It reduces the chance of wasted matings and wasted energy. A weak or sick animal is less likely to win a mate.

title: Parental Care in Animals
summary: The link between the number of young and the amount of care, with examples from fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

p: Parental care means any time, energy or food that parents give to help their young to survive: guarding eggs, building nests, keeping young warm, feeding and protecting them, and teaching them.

Low parental care means many eggs. If the parents do not look after the young, most are eaten or die, so thousands of eggs must be made so that a few survive (fish, amphibians). High parental care means few young, because most survive when protected (birds, mammals). That is why a female fish lays thousands of eggs, while a cow gives birth to only one calf a year.

sections.h: Patterns of care in the animal classes
p: Fish: most lay eggs and leave them. Exception: tilapia is a mouth brooder: the female keeps the fertilised eggs, and later the young, in her mouth until they can fend for themselves. The male seahorse carries the eggs in a brood pouch.
Amphibians: toads and frogs lay jelly-covered eggs in water and leave them; the tadpoles live alone. Exception: the male midwife toad carries strings of eggs wound round his legs.
Reptiles: most bury their leathery eggs in sand or soil and leave. Exception: the female crocodile guards her nest fiercely and carries the hatchlings to the water in her mouth.

Birds: high care. They build nests (the weaver bird weaves a hanging nest), incubate the eggs to keep them warm, feed the chicks with insects, worms or seeds, and defend them. A hen covers her chicks with her wings and scratches the ground to show them food.

Mammals: the highest care. Young are born alive (viviparous), fed with milk (lactation), protected for months or years and taught skills, such as lions teaching cubs to hunt, and humans teaching children.

sections.h: Comparing a toad and a cat
p: Toad: thousands of eggs, external fertilisation, no parental care. Cat: a few kittens (3 to 5) in a litter, internal fertilisation and development in the uterus, high care with milk and protection.

The cuckoo, a brood parasite, lays its eggs in the nests of other birds, which then bring up the cuckoo chick as their own. The host wastes its energy and food on a stranger, and the cuckoo chick may push the host's own eggs or chicks out of the nest. In Nigeria, honeyguides and whydahs (viduine finches) are also brood parasites.

It ensures that the species continues; passes on good genes; and increases the survival of young so that the population stays steady. Parental care is a sacrifice: the parents spend a lot of energy and food, are more at risk from predators and may lose weight.

activity: Observe a hen with chicks and report on how she protects and feeds them. Make a table comparing a toad and a cat (number of young, fertilisation, care). Define mouth brooding and name an animal that does it. Discuss the statement 'parental care is a sacrifice'.

title: Third Term Revision and Exam Practice
summary: A checklist for the term's nervous system, sense organs, population ecology, ecosystems, human reproduction, seeds and fruits, and animal behaviour, with worked answers.

p: Nervous coordination: neuron parts; resting and action potential; saltatory conduction; synapse; brain and spinal cord; autonomic nervous system; reflex arc.
Sense organs: eye (parts, accommodation, defects); ear (hearing and balance); nose, tongue and skin.
Population ecology: density, frequency, distribution; natality, mortality, immigration and emigration; growth curves; limiting factors; quadrat and capture-mark-recapture.
Ecosystem: components; food chain and web; the 10% rule; pyramids; carbon and water cycles; balance of nature.
Human reproduction: male and female systems; gametes; menstrual cycle; fertilisation, pregnancy and birth.
Plants: fertilisation; seed structure; germination; fruit types and dispersal.
Behaviour: courtship and parental care.
Why is a myelinated neuron faster? The action potential jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction) instead of travelling along the whole length of the axon.
What happens in the cerebellum damage? The person has jerky movements, loss of balance and poor coordination.
Calculation: 40 marked, second catch 60 with 12 marked: N = 40 × 60 ÷ 12 = 200.
Why does a pyramid of energy always stand upright? Energy is lost at every level (only about 10% passes on), so each level has less energy than the one below.
Why are the testes outside the body? Sperm need a temperature 2 to 3 °C lower than the body.
What is the function of the micropyle in a dry seed? It lets water and air enter when germination starts.
Why is a maize grain called a fruit? The fruit wall (pericarp) is fused to the seed coat.
Why does a female fish lay thousands of eggs and a cow one calf? Fish give no care, so most eggs are lost; a cow gives much care, so most calves survive.

Diagrams: neuron, reflex arc, brain, eye, ear, male and female systems, bean seed, maize grain, food web, S-curve. Calculations: population density and capture-recapture. Practicals: blind-spot test, quadrat count, germination experiment.
